newsitem.title: USA: National Pork Board backs audit of checkoff funds.
newsitem.headline: National Pork Board backs audit of checkoff funds.

text.p: The National Pork Board said it would support a U.S. Agriculture Department audit of its funds to clear up allegations that it spent money to investigate environmentalists and animal rights groups.

In a letter to USDA Assistant Secretary of Marketing and Regulatory Programs Mike Dunn, Pork Board president Carnell Korsmeyer said an audit would show that the board's use of "checkoff" funds had been consistent with the Pork Act.

"I would support it in the belief that it will verify that our business and accounting systems are working properly and that producer checkoff dollars are being spent consistent with the Pork Act and Pork Order," Korsmeyer said.

Under the federal Pork Act, 45 cents of every $100 of pork sold in the United States goes to the Pork Board as "checkoff" funds which it uses to support pork industry promotion, research and consumer information.

Controversy arose this year when the National Pork Producers Council, which receives checkoff funds from the board, said it hired the Washington, D.C., firm of Mongoven Biscoe & Duchin Inc in 1996 to monitor groups involved in environmental, animal rights, industry structure and food safety issues.
On March 7, outgoing NPPC president Bob Ruggles told the group's annual meeting in Atlanta the NPPC had not investigated any activist groups.
"There was and is no ongoing investigation of any of those groups or any other group by NPPC," Ruggles said.
Ruggles said one report to NPPC by Mongoven in 1996 centered on activist groups in the forefront of changes in the pork industry. He said the report was not funded by checkoff funds.
But he said he had apologized to one organization, the Natinal Farmers Union, when he discovered it had been included in the Mongoven report.

The Mongoven firm was hired under an NPPC program, the Strategic Communications Initiative, aimed at pursuing what the NPPC called "accurate and fair reporting and coverage" of the pork industry, particularly by the news media.
Consumer groups have continued to press for an accounting of how all checkoff funds were used.

"Checkoff funds, paid by family farmers, are being used to investigate the activities of organizations involving those same family farmers in efforts to enhance their farm future," Chuck Hassebrook of the Center for Rural Affairs said last week.

On March 28, the Agriculture Department ordered the Pork Board to recover any checkoff funds improperly spent. Under the Pork Act, the USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service oversees the activities of the National Pork Board.
